title: Alleged victim speaks out after former Coffee Co. deputy accused of tracking her is released on bond

reading.body:
This is an insider misuse case rather than a model failure. A sworn officer with legitimate access to three law enforcement systems, the Flock camera network, a tag reader system, and the Georgia Crime Information Center database, is accused of querying them for personal reasons over a two month period, including tracking a woman without her consent. The systems performed as designed: they returned location and identity data to a credentialed user. The failure sits at the point of access, not in the software.

Controls that would catch this are audit and purpose limitation. Camera and plate reader networks log every query against an operator identity, and a review that compares query patterns to case numbers or dispatch records can surface lookups with no investigative basis. The GCIC database carries its own access rules and audit trail. Catching misuse of this kind requires someone reading those logs, or a colleague or supervisor noticing queries that do not match any open case.

The indictment is an allegation, and the eight counts have not been tested at trial. Rozar was fired when the investigation began, was arrested on May 5 and released on bond the same day, and his arraignment is scheduled for May 27 in Coffee County Superior Court. Whether he in fact used the systems for personal reasons is not established by the reporting.

reports.title: Alleged victim speaks out after former Coffee Co. deputy accused of tracking her is released on bond

summary:
A former Coffee County sheriff's deputy, Chris Ashley Rozar, has been released on bond after a grand jury indicted him on eight counts, including four counts of violating his oath, two counts of computer invasion of privacy, one count of prohibited use of captured license plate data, and one count of stalking. Prosecutors say the 49-year-old misused the sheriff's office Flock camera system, tag reader system, and the Georgia Crime Information Center database for personal reasons between April 2024 and May 2024, including tracking a woman without her consent.

The woman, who asked to remain anonymous, said she hopes speaking out encourages other women to report abuse. The Georgia Bureau of Investigation led the multi-year investigation after former Sheriff Doyle Wooten requested it in 2024, and Rozar was fired when it began. He was arrested on May 5 and released on bond the same day. His arraignment is scheduled for May 27 in Coffee County Superior Court.
